prompt: You run `redis:7.2` as a container named `cache` and want to move to `redis:7.4`.

`docker stop cache`
`docker rm cache`
`docker run -d --name cache redis:7.4` (same flags and volume as before)
`docker logs cache` to check it started cleanly

prompt: Your container stops as soon as it starts.

task.prompt: You run `docker run -d --name web my-app:1.0`. A second later `docker ps` shows nothing.

steps.question: What do you run first?
options: `docker ps -a` and `docker logs web`
`docker rmi my-app:1.0` and rebuild
Restart the Docker daemon
`docker run` again with `--restart always`
steps.explanation: `ps -a` shows stopped containers and the exit code; `logs` shows what the app printed before it died.

steps.question: The logs say `Error: DATABASE_URL is not set`. What is the fix?
options: Pass it in: `-e DATABASE_URL=...` or `--env-file .env`
Add `EXPOSE 5432` to the image
Run with `-it` instead of `-d`
Use `--restart unless-stopped` so it retries
steps.explanation: The app needs configuration the container never received. Environment variables are passed at `docker run` time.

prompt: An onboarding note about Docker basics.

task.prompt: Mark the sentences that are wrong.

segments.text: An image is a read-only template; a container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image.
You can start many containers from the same image.
Deleting a container also deletes the image it was started from.
segments.issue: Removing a container leaves the image in place; `docker rmi` removes images.

segments.text: `docker ps` lists running containers; add `-a` to include stopped ones.
Files a container writes outside a volume survive `docker rm`.
segments.issue: The container's writable layer is deleted with the container; use a volume to keep data.

segments.text: `docker pull` downloads an image from a registry such as Docker Hub.

prompt: What does `docker run -p 8080:80 nginx` do with the ports?

options: Traffic to port 8080 on the host goes to port 80 in the container
Traffic to port 80 on the host goes to port 8080 in the container
The container listens on both 8080 and 80
It only documents the ports; nothing is published
mcq.explanation: The format is `host:container`. Browse to `localhost:8080` to reach nginx listening on 80 inside the container.

prompt: Which statement about images and containers is right?

options: A container is a running instance of an image; one image can back many containers
An image is a running container that has been paused
Each image can only be used for one container
Containers are stored in a registry, images live only on your laptop
mcq.explanation: Images are templates (pushed to registries); containers are instances created from them, as many as you like.

prompt: Your container crashed and `docker ps` shows nothing. How do you see it?

options: `docker ps -a`
`docker images`
`docker inspect --running`
`docker logs --all`
mcq.explanation: `docker ps` lists only running containers. `-a` includes stopped and exited ones with their exit status.

prompt: You ran `docker ps -a --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}'`. Complete `runningNames` so it returns the names of containers whose status starts with `Up`, in order. Output can be empty.

args:
api	Up 3 hours

prompt: `docker system df` prints sizes like `350MB`, `1.2GB`, `512kB` or `0B`. Complete `to_mb` so it returns the size in megabytes (Docker uses 1000, not 1024).
This command runs Postgres on a shared staging server.

task.prompt: Mark the flags that are a problem on a shared server.

segments.issue: A literal password ends up in shell history and in `docker inspect`; use `--env-file` or a secret file.
Publishes the database on every interface of the server; bind to `127.0.0.1:5432:5432` or keep it on a private network.
`latest` changes under you; a major Postgres upgrade cannot read the old data directory. Pin `postgres:16`.

prompt: The server's disk is nearly full and Docker is the culprit.

task.prompt: Order these from what to run first (safest) to last (most destructive).

items.label: `docker system df` to see what is using space
`docker container prune` (stopped containers)
`docker image prune` (dangling images only)
`docker image prune -a` (every image no container uses)
`docker volume prune` (unused volumes, which may hold data)

task.explanation: Measure first, then remove things that are cheap to recreate. Volumes go last because they can hold data that cannot be recreated.

prompt: Database data disappeared after an update.

task.prompt: Someone updated Postgres with `docker rm -f db` and `docker run -d --name db postgres:16`. All tables are gone.

steps.question: Why did the data disappear?
options: The data lived in the old container's writable layer, removed with the container
Postgres 16 deletes data from older versions
`-f` wipes the image cache
The image was pulled again from scratch
steps.explanation: Without a volume, the data directory is part of the container and goes away with `docker rm`.

steps.question: How should the database be run from now on?
options: Mount a named volume at the data directory: `-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data`
Never remove the container; only restart it
Commit the container to an image after each change
Copy the data out with `docker cp` once a day
steps.explanation: A volume lives outside any container, so you can replace the container freely and the data stays.

prompt: Your API container cannot reach the database.

task.prompt: The API runs in one container and Postgres in another, both started with plain `docker run`. The API's `DATABASE_URL` uses `localhost:5432` and gets `ECONNREFUSED`.

steps.question: Why does `localhost` fail?
options: Inside a container, `localhost` is the container itself, not the host or other containers
Postgres does not accept TCP connections by default
Port 5432 is reserved by Docker
The API needs `--privileged` to open sockets
steps.explanation: Each container has its own network namespace and loopback interface.

steps.question: What is the clean fix?
options: Create a network (`docker network create app`), run both with `--network app`, and use `db:5432`
Use the container's IP from `docker inspect` in `DATABASE_URL`
Publish 5432 and hardcode the host's public IP
Run both processes in one container
steps.explanation: On a user-defined network, Docker's DNS resolves container names, and IPs can change on restart.

prompt: What is the difference between `docker run` and `docker exec`?

options: `run` creates and starts a new container; `exec` runs a command inside an already running container
`exec` creates a new container from an image; `run` re-runs the last command
They are aliases
`exec` only works on stopped containers
mcq.explanation: Use `docker exec -it <name> sh` to look around inside a running container; `docker run` always makes a new one.

prompt: What does `docker logs api` show?

options: What the container's main process wrote to stdout and stderr
Every file under `/var/log` inside the container
The Docker daemon's own log
The build output of the image
mcq.explanation: Docker captures the main process's stdout/stderr. Apps that log to files inside the container will not show up, which is why containerised apps log to stdout.

prompt: A teammate runs `docker run -e API_KEY=abc123 my-app`. Where can someone else on that machine see the key?

options: In `docker inspect` output for the container, and in the shell history
Nowhere; `-e` values are encrypted
Only inside the container
Only in the image layers on Docker Hub
mcq.explanation: Environment variables are stored in the container config and shown by `docker inspect`. Use `--env-file` (kept out of git) or mounted secret files.

task.prompt: Mark the flags that give the container far more power than it needs.

segments.issue: Turns off nearly all isolation: every device and capability on the host.
The Docker socket is root on the host; a compromised shipper can start any container.
Shares the host's network stack; the shipper only needs outbound traffic.

prompt: A container keeps restarting. Work it out the usual way.

items.label: `docker ps -a` to see the status and exit code
`docker logs --tail 100 <name>` to read the last output
`docker inspect <name>` to check env, mounts, command and `OOMKilled`
`docker run -it --entrypoint sh <image>` to poke around the image by hand
Fix the cause, rebuild or reconfigure, and watch it stay up

task.explanation: Cheap, read-only checks first; the exit code and logs usually explain it. Inspect for configuration, then a shell for anything still unclear.

prompt: A worker container dies with exit code 137.

task.prompt: `docker ps -a` shows `worker  Exited (137) 3 minutes ago`. It happens under load.

steps.question: What does 137 usually mean?
options: The process was killed with SIGKILL (128 + 9), often by the out-of-memory killer
The app returned an error code 137 on purpose
The image is for a different CPU
The container could not bind its port
steps.explanation: Exit codes above 128 mean killed by a signal; 9 is SIGKILL. Check `docker inspect` for `"OOMKilled": true`.

steps.question: `docker inspect` shows `OOMKilled: true` and `--memory 256m`. What is the right next step?
options: Check real memory use (`docker stats`) and either raise the limit or fix the leak
Remove the memory limit entirely in production
Add `--restart always` so it comes back
Switch to an Alpine base image
steps.explanation: Restarting hides the problem; removing the limit lets one container starve the host. Measure, then size the limit or fix the leak.

prompt: An image works on your laptop but not on the server.

task.prompt: You built `api:1.3` on an Apple Silicon Mac and pushed it. On the x86 EC2 server the container exits immediately with `exec format error`.

steps.question: What is the cause?
options: The image was built for arm64 and the server is amd64
The server's Docker version is too old
The entrypoint script has Windows line endings
The server is out of disk space
steps.explanation: `exec format error` means the binary is for another CPU architecture.

steps.question: How do you fix it for good?
options: Build for the server's platform, e.g. `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64` (or both platforms), ideally in CI
Run the container with `--privileged`
Rename the tag to `api:1.3-x86`
Install Rosetta on the server
steps.explanation: buildx can build for another platform or a multi-arch image; building in CI on the target platform avoids laptop-specific images.

prompt: `docker stop api` always takes about 10 seconds before the container stops. What is the most likely reason?

options: The main process ignores SIGTERM, so Docker waits 10 s and then sends SIGKILL
Docker always waits 10 s to flush logs
The container has too little memory
The image is too large to unload quickly
mcq.explanation: `docker stop` sends SIGTERM, waits (10 s default) and then kills. A shell wrapper as PID 1 that does not forward signals is the usual cause; use exec form or `--init`.

prompt: What does the `latest` tag guarantee?

options: Nothing special: it is just the default tag name used when none is given
That it is the newest image pushed to the repository
That the image has passed security scanning
That the image will never change
mcq.explanation: `latest` is only whatever was last pushed with that tag (or nothing). Pin explicit versions for anything you deploy.

prompt: You are developing locally and want code changes on your laptop to show up in the container instantly. Which mount fits?

options: A bind mount of the source folder, e.g. `-v $(pwd)/src:/app/src`
A named volume, e.g. `-v appsrc:/app/src`
A `tmpfs` mount at `/app/src`
No mount; rebuild the image on each save
mcq.explanation: Bind mounts map a host path into the container, so edits are visible immediately. Named volumes are managed by Docker and suit data like databases.

prompt: Complete `parseImage` so it splits an image reference into `{ registry, repository, tag }` the way Docker does: the first part is a registry only if it contains `.` or `:` or is `localhost`; otherwise the registry is `docker.io`, and single-name images get the `library/` prefix. The tag defaults to `latest`.

A cleanup job keeps the `keep` newest images **per repository** and deletes the rest. Each image is `{"repo", "tag", "created"}` (created is a unix time). Fix `to_delete` so it returns `repo:tag` strings to delete, sorted alphabetically.
The runbook for new Docker hosts.

task.prompt: Mark the steps that are dangerous.

segments.text: Install Docker Engine from Docker's official apt repository.
Enable the remote API on `tcp://0.0.0.0:2375` so CI can deploy.
segments.issue: An unauthenticated Docker API on the network is root on the host for anyone who reaches it; use an SSH context or TLS.

segments.text: Deploy by pulling `:latest` on every server so all hosts stay current.
segments.issue: Not reproducible: hosts can end up on different builds and you cannot roll back to a known tag. Deploy immutable tags.

segments.text: Mount secrets as read-only files rather than environment variables.
Run `docker system prune -a --volumes -f` nightly from cron.

prompt: You deploy a containerised API on a single host behind nginx and want zero downtime.

items.label: Build and push an image tagged with the git sha
Pull the new image on the host
Start the new container next to the old one on a different port
Wait until its health check passes
Point the nginx upstream at the new container and reload nginx
Stop and remove the old container

task.explanation: The old container keeps serving until the new one is proven healthy and traffic has moved. Only then remove it, which also leaves a quick rollback path until the last step.

prompt: A production host ran out of disk.

task.prompt: Alerts fire: `/` is 100% full on a Docker host. Containers have been up for months.

steps.question: Where do you look first?
options: `docker system df -v` and `du -sh /var/lib/docker/containers/*` to find large container logs
Delete `/var/lib/docker` and restart Docker
Run `docker volume prune -f`
Reboot the host
steps.explanation: Unbounded `json-file` logs under `/var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/` are the classic cause. Measure before deleting anything.

steps.question: One container's `-json.log` is 40 GB. What is the long-term fix?
options: Set log rotation (`max-size`, `max-file`) in `daemon.json` or on the container
Add a cron job that deletes the log file
Turn logging off with `--log-driver none` everywhere
Move `/var/lib/docker` to a bigger disk and stop there
steps.explanation: Rotation keeps the logs useful and bounded. Deleting an open file does not free space, and disabling logs loses them.

steps.question: You updated `daemon.json`. Why is the big container still not rotating?
options: Log options apply to containers created after the change, so it must be recreated
The daemon ignores `daemon.json` for running hosts
Rotation only works with Alpine images
You also need `--privileged`
steps.explanation: Log settings are fixed at container creation. Recreate the container (same image and flags) to pick them up.

prompt: A bad release needs rolling back.

task.prompt: Your servers run `api:latest`. The new build broke checkout, and the previous build was also pushed as `api:latest`.

steps.question: How do you find the previous image to roll back to?
options: Look up its digest or sha tag in the registry or CI history, then run that exact reference
Run `docker pull api:latest` again
Use `docker rollback api`
Rebuild the old commit and hope it matches
steps.explanation: Once a tag is overwritten, only digests or other tags identify the old image. `docker rollback` does not exist.

steps.question: What process change prevents this next time?
options: Tag every image with an immutable version (git sha or semver) and deploy that tag
Keep using `latest` but add a second `latest-old` tag
Disable image pulls on servers
Only deploy on Fridays
steps.explanation: Immutable tags make every deploy and rollback a specific, reproducible image.

prompt: A container runs as `root` (the default) with `-v /etc:/host-etc`. What can its process do?

options: Edit the host's `/etc` as root, since container root maps to host root without user-namespace remapping
Nothing on the host, because containers are fully isolated from the host's files
Only read the files; bind mounts are always read-only
Write only files it created itself
mcq.explanation: By default UID 0 in the container is UID 0 on the host. Bind mounts expose host files with those permissions; run as a non-root user and mount `:ro` where possible.

prompt: What is the difference between `--restart always` and `--restart unless-stopped`?

options: `unless-stopped` will not bring a container back after the daemon restarts if you had stopped it manually; `always` will
`always` restarts only on non-zero exit codes
`unless-stopped` never restarts after a crash
They are identical
mcq.explanation: Both restart after crashes. After a daemon or host restart, `always` starts every such container, while `unless-stopped` respects a manual `docker stop`.

prompt: Why pin an image as `node@sha256:<digest>` instead of `node:20`?

options: A digest always refers to the exact same image bytes; a tag can be moved to a new image
Digests download faster
Tags cannot be used in production
A digest also pins the host's Docker version
mcq.explanation: Tags are mutable pointers (`node:20` gets new patch releases). A digest is content-addressed, so builds and deploys are reproducible; update it deliberately.
